transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. It's really nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. 

I, um... I guess I'm here because I've been having a little bit of trouble at work lately. It's probably just stress or something, I don't want to make a huge deal out of it, but... my mind keeps sort of going blank at the worst possible times. 

I'm a flagger, and sometimes I'll look at the road-closure forms, or even just be holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just... I can't remember the steps. Things I've done perfectly for years. It's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly. I hope it's okay that I made an appointment for this? I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by coming in to get it checked out.
When your mind goes blank like that, does it feel like you are watching yourself from outside your body or that the world around you seems unreal?

No, it's not really like that. I don't feel like I'm outside my body or anything strange like that. It's just... I just lose my train of thought. It's totally normal, right? Like, everyone gets a little foggy sometimes when they're tired or stressed. I'm sure I'm just overreacting by even mentioning it. I just want to be doing a good job, you know? Is it helpful that I'm telling you this, or am I just wasting your time with the little things?
When these episodes of your mind going blank happen, do you notice your heart racing, sweating, or any physical shaking?

No, no, nothing like that. I'm not... I don't get panicky or shaky or anything. My heart doesn't race. It's really just a quiet sort of blankness, you know? Just a little slip of the mind. 

I try really hard to stay calm at work, so I definitely don't have any big physical reactions like sweating or shaking. I wouldn't want to cause a scene or make my coworkers worry. I'm pretty good at keeping it together on the outside. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your questions right. I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.
During these moments when your mind goes blank, do you ever experience any unusual tastes, smells, or repetitive movements like lip-smacking or picking at your clothes?

No, no, I definitely don't do any of that. I don't smell anything weird or taste anything, and I... I don't do any weird movements like smacking my lips or picking at things. I'm very professional at work, I promise. I just stand there holding my sign, trying to remember what I'm supposed to do next. 

I wouldn't want anyone to think I was acting strangely or unprofessionally out there. I hope it's okay that I don't have those symptoms? I know you're trying to figure this out, and I really want to be helpful... I just haven't noticed anything like that at all. Is that an okay answer?
Have you noticed any other physical symptoms lately, such as unusual fatigue, headaches, changes in your vision, or any recent illnesses?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I get a little tired sometimes, but who doesn't, right? Standing outside all day can be exhausting, but I don't think it's anything unusual. No headaches or vision changes, and I haven't been sick at all. 

I try to take really good care of myself so I don't miss work. I know they rely on me, and I want to be reliable. So, physically, I think I'm doing just fine. I hope that's helpful? I don't want to be missing anything important that you need to know.
Outside of those moments where your mind goes blank, do you feel like you are constantly struggling with a sense of mental exhaustion or difficulty concentrating throughout your day?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm constantly exhausted or struggling all day. I try really hard to stay focused and do a good job. It's just... well, honestly, the main reason I came in is because of those blank moments. 

It's just so embarrassing. I'll be out there, and I'll look at the road-closure forms, or even just hold my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly... I just can't remember the steps. And I've done this for years! I know how to do my job, I promise I do. It just slips away right at the worst times. 

I hope it doesn't make me sound incompetent. I really do try my best to be good at my job. Does that make sense? I'm sorry if I'm not explaining it very well.
When these blank moments occur, do they come on and resolve suddenly, or do they feel more like a gradual drift in your concentration?

Well, it's... it's really sudden. That's what makes it so embarrassing. I'll be completely fine, just doing my job, and then—bam. It's like someone just unplugs my brain. 

Like I said, I'll be looking right at the road-closure forms, or holding my paddle, and in an instant, I just... I cannot remember the steps. And these are things I have done for years. It's not like I'm gradually losing focus or getting distracted by something else. It just vanishes all at once. 

Then, after a minute or two, it comes back, and I try to act like nothing happened so nobody worries. I hope that's the kind of detail you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information so you can help me figure this out.
During these moments when your mind goes blank, are you aware of what is happening around you, or is there a period of time that you simply cannot account for?

Oh, no, no, I'm definitely still aware of everything around me. I don't... I don't black out or lose time or anything scary like that. 

I can still see the cars waiting, and I hear the construction crew, and I know exactly where I am. It's really just... the specific steps of what I'm supposed to be doing right in that second just sort of vanish from my head. But I'm fully awake and present. 

I would never want to put anyone in danger out on the road, so I'm very glad it's not like I'm completely losing consciousness or anything. I'm right there, just... stuck for a second. 

Is that what you were asking? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of answers. I just want to be really clear that I'm still paying attention to my surroundings when it happens.
Did these episodes of going blank start around the same time as any significant change or stressful event in your personal life?

Well, um... yes, actually. I guess it was a pretty stressful time. It started about a year and eight months ago. 

I... I lost my closest friend right around then. She passed away, and it was really hard on me. I tried my best to keep it together, you know, to not let it affect my work or anything. I really didn't want to be a burden to anyone or make a big deal out of it. But I suppose that's when these blank moments started happening. 

I hope it doesn't seem like I'm just making excuses or letting my personal life get in the way of my job. I really try to keep them separate. Do you think that could be what caused all this? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right pieces of the puzzle so you can help me fix it.
Are you still feeling significantly distressed or preoccupied by the loss of your friend, or do you feel like you have mostly moved past that emotional pain?

Well, um... I guess I'd say I'm trying really hard to move past it. I really am. I don't want to be someone who just dwells on things and brings everyone else down, you know? 

But... if I'm being completely honest, and I know I should be so you can help me... it's still really hard. Most mornings, I wake up with this... this heavy, hollow sadness right in my chest. It's almost like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor. 

I try to shake it off, I really do, because I know I need to get to work and do a good job. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just wallowing in it or not trying hard enough to get better. I just... I still feel it pretty strongly. Is that normal to still feel that way after all this time? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how things are going.
Outside of the sadness you described, have you lost interest or pleasure in the hobbies or activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, um... I guess... maybe a little bit? I don't want to sound like I'm just being lazy or giving up on things. I used to be so involved in my community, you know? I was always the one organizing the carpools for the church choir, and setting up the neighborhood garden swaps, and making sure all the kids had snacks for youth basketball. I really loved doing all of that, and I hope people know I still care about them.

But lately... well, for a while now... I just don't have that same energy for it. I feel terrible admitting this, but sometimes I can just sit for hours on my couch, just staring at my phone, and I see the messages coming in from people, but I just... I don't feel that push to answer anyone. It's not that I don't like them anymore! I just can't seem to make myself do the things I used to do. 

I hope you don't think I'm just being antisocial or ignoring my friends on purpose. I feel really guilty about it. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your question the right way.

Have you experienced these periods of feeling this way, where you lose interest in things and feel that heavy sadness, at any other times in your life before this, or has this been one long, continuous period since your friend passed away?

Well, um... I guess it hasn't been one continuous thing since she passed. For the first few months after it happened, I really tried to push through it. I was doing okay, I think. But then... well, it's been about a year and two months now that I've been stuck in this really deep rut. 

That's when the heavy sadness really set in, and I started feeling so guilty all the time... and my energy just bottomed out. I even stopped wanting to eat much, which I know isn't good. I really try to force myself to have something, so I don't want you to think I'm doing it on purpose. But it's just been this one long, really hard stretch for the last fourteen months or so. 

I hope it's okay that I didn't feel it right away... I don't want it to seem like I didn't care about her at first. Does that timeline make sense to you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of the symptoms and whether they started around a significant change or stressful event. This matches the 'Duration' profile, which details that the symptoms started about a year and eight months ago after the patient's closest friend died.

patient.answer:
Well, um... yes, actually. I guess it was a pretty stressful time. It started about a year and eight months ago. 

I... I lost my closest friend right around then. She passed away, and it was really hard on me. I tried my best to keep it together, you know, to not let it affect my work or anything. I really didn't want to be a burden to anyone or make a big deal out of it. But I suppose that's when these blank moments started happening. 

I hope it doesn't seem like I'm just making excuses or letting my personal life get in the way of my job. I really try to keep them separate. Do you think that could be what caused all this? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right pieces of the puzzle so you can help me fix it.

inference.note: The patient's description of sudden, transient episodes of 'blanking' while maintaining full awareness, combined with the onset following a significant bereavement, makes an anxiety-based dissociation (F48.0) or an adjustment disorder (F43.2) more likely than generalized anxiety (F41.8). The lack of autonomic arousal or loss of consciousness helps rule out panic disorder or typical absence seizures.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between adjustment disorder (F43.2) and neurasthenia/fatigue syndrome (F48.0) by assessing if the symptoms are currently tied to the distress of the life event or if they have become a persistent, generalized pattern of mental fatigue.
doctor.question: Are you still feeling significantly distressed or preoccupied by the loss of your friend, or do you feel like you have mostly moved past that emotional pain?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the emotional pain and distress from the loss are still present, which directly inquires about the persistence of a depressed or sad mood.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess I'd say I'm trying really hard to move past it. I really am. I don't want to be someone who just dwells on things and brings everyone else down, you know? 

But... if I'm being completely honest, and I know I should be so you can help me... it's still really hard. Most mornings, I wake up with this... this heavy, hollow sadness right in my chest. It's almost like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor. 

I try to shake it off, I really do, because I know I need to get to work and do a good job. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just wallowing in it or not trying hard enough to get better. I just... I still feel it pretty strongly. Is that normal to still feel that way after all this time? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how things are going.

inference.note: The patient's persistent, significant symptoms of sadness and impairment following a loss, lasting over 1.5 years, point towards persistent complex bereavement disorder or a depressive episode rather than simple adjustment disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient meets the criteria for a major depressive episode, specifically regarding anhedonia or loss of interest in activities.
doctor.question: Outside of the sadness you described, have you lost interest or pleasure in the hobbies or activities that you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the one organizing choir rides, garden swaps, and youth basketball snacks, but now I can sit for hours staring at my phone and not feel the push to answer anybody.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed hobbies or activities, which aligns with the diminished motivation and social interest described in the Negative Symptoms profile.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess... maybe a little bit? I don't want to sound like I'm just being lazy or giving up on things. I used to be so involved in my community, you know? I was always the one organizing the carpools for the church choir, and setting up the neighborhood garden swaps, and making sure all the kids had snacks for youth basketball. I really loved doing all of that, and I hope people know I still care about them.

But lately... well, for a while now... I just don't have that same energy for it. I feel terrible admitting this, but sometimes I can just sit for hours on my couch, just staring at my phone, and I see the messages coming in from people, but I just... I don't feel that push to answer anyone. It's not that I don't like them anymore! I just can't seem to make myself do the things I used to do. 

I hope you don't think I'm just being antisocial or ignoring my friends on purpose. I feel really guilty about it. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your question the right way.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms (anhedonia, persistent sadness, cognitive 'fogginess', and social withdrawal) persisting for nearly two years are more consistent with a depressive disorder than an adjustment disorder. The 'blank moments' appear to be manifestations of psychomotor retardation or concentration deficits associated with a major depressive episode.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced these symptoms as a single, isolated episode or as recurring episodes over time to differentiate between a single major depressive episode and recurrent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you experienced these periods of feeling this way, where you lose interest in things and feel that heavy sadness, at any other times in your life before this, or has this been one long, continuous period since your friend passed away?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The heavy depression, guilt, low energy, and loss of appetite have been with me for about a year and two months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and continuity of the depressive symptoms (heavy sadness and loss of interest). The 'depressive_episode_duration' item directly addresses how long these specific symptoms have been present.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess it hasn't been one continuous thing since she passed. For the first few months after it happened, I really tried to push through it. I was doing okay, I think. But then... well, it's been about a year and two months now that I've been stuck in this really deep rut. 

That's when the heavy sadness really set in, and I started feeling so guilty all the time... and my energy just bottomed out. I even stopped wanting to eat much, which I know isn't good. I really try to force myself to have something, so I don't want you to think I'm doing it on purpose. But it's just been this one long, really hard stretch for the last fourteen months or so. 

I hope it's okay that I didn't feel it right away... I don't want it to seem like I didn't care about her at first. Does that timeline make sense to you? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

inference.note: The patient describes a 14-month duration of depressive symptoms (anhedonia, persistent low mood, loss of energy, appetite changes, and guilt), which fits the criteria for Recurrent Depressive Disorder (F33.x). Given the severity and duration without a prior episode of mania, F33.1 (Recurrent depressive disorder, current moderate episode) is the most appropriate diagnostic candidate.

As the patient notes this is a recurrent pattern of being 'stuck' in this state, and distinguishes it from previous periods of functioning, it aligns with Recurrent Depressive Disorder.
